reference.title: used to / didn’t use to
rows: When I was a child I used to play in the streets.
My brother used to have very long hair when he was a student.
Nick didn’t use to go out much, but now he goes out every night.
I didn’t use to like vegetables, but now I love them.
Did you use to wear a uniform at school? Yes, I did.
Did you use to like your teachers? No, I didn’t.

reference.text: We use used to / didn’t use to + verb for things that happened repeatedly or were true for a long time in the past, and usually are not true now. used to is the same for all persons (I / you / he / she / we / they used to). We can also use the past simple, often with an adverb of frequency: When I was a child I often played in the street.

reference.wrong: I didn’t used to like maths. Did you used to like maths?
reference.right: I didn’t use to like maths. Did you use to like maths?
reference.why: After didn’t and did we write use to, without -d.

reference.wrong: I use to cook in the evenings.
reference.right: I usually cook in the evenings.
reference.why: used to is only for the past. For present habits we use usually + present simple.

reference.title: Fame Academy
reference.text: Three famous people’s teachers remember them at school. Alex Turner (Arctic Monkeys) was very popular and loved sport, not music. J.K. Rowling was a very quiet child; her mum was seriously ill. Jude Law was clever and confident, but some teachers and classmates thought he was arrogant.

reference.title: Glossary
reference.text: Professor Snape – the potions teacher in the Harry Potter books. housemaster – teacher in charge of a house in a boarding school. be bullied – be badly treated physically or mentally by other people, e.g. by other children at school.

tasks.instruction: Read the article ‘Fame Academy’. When they were at school, who was the most popular, the most unpopular, and the quietest student?
tasks.context:
Alex Turner – Mark Coleman, his PE teacher
Everyone liked Alex at school. He was very good at English. Mr Baker, his English teacher, really liked poetry, and I’m sure Alex was inspired by him because his song lyrics are incredible. But he didn’t use to be very interested in music, he was much more interested in sports – he was possibly the best in the school at basketball. When he was 14 he broke his arm in my PE lesson. He was in hospital for a week, and we collected money and bought him a CD, so he was probably beginning to get interested in music. Everyone at the school is very proud of the band, and I’m sometimes invited to their concerts.

J.K. Rowling – John Nettleship, her science teacher
Joanne was about 12 when I taught her. Her school days weren’t very happy. The school was a bit like a prison, and then her mum, Anne, got seriously ill. Anne worked as my technician, and Joanne used to come and wait outside the science building for her mum, so that they could walk home together. She was obviously very worried about her mum. She was a very quiet child. I don’t remember her ever answering a question. I think she was keeping all her experiences in her head to use later in her stories. Joanne has said that no characters in Harry Potter are based more than 10% on a real person. So perhaps it’s just a coincidence that I used to have long, black hair. But to be honest, I think Professor Snape, especially in the later books, is very like me.

Jude Law – Mike Jones, his housemaster
Jude was bullied at his first secondary school so he changed schools when he was 14 and came to us. He didn’t know anybody, but that wasn’t a problem for him. He adapted very quickly, which shows his confidence. He quickly started acting in school plays, and he used to get fantastic reviews in the school magazine. He was clever, but some teachers thought he was arrogant. Some of his classmates thought the same and he wasn’t very popular with them. Other boys were jealous of him because the girls usually liked him.
